messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: vectorization etc.
parts:
Hi folks,

I've been playing around with a template metaprogramming scheme that
may allow us to automatically generate
vectorized/mixed-type-specialized functions without having to rewrite
everything a million times. The mixed-type side is already partly
done—I've rewritten a bunch of partials_vari.hpp so that the ad
nauseum specializations of simple_var aren't necessary.

Just a heads up that if all goes well then it may not be necessary to
spend a bunch of time grinding on specialized implementations.

Matt

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] vectorization etc.
parts:
It's true that you can't template out variable declarations, so
instead I used arrays whose lengths are known at compile time. The
partials3_vari class illustrates the basic idea:

template <typename T1, typename T2, typename T3>
class partials3_vari : public vari {
private:
const static size_t nvars_ = !stan::is_constant<T1>::value +
!stan::is_constant<T2>::value +
!stan::is_constant<T3>::value;
vari* operands_[nvars_];
double partials_[nvars_];

public:
partials3_vari(double value,
T1 operand1, double partial1,
T2 operand2, double partial2,
T3 operand3, double partial3)
: vari(value) {
size_t i = 0;
if (!stan::is_constant<T1>::value) {
operands_[i] = *(vari**)(&operand1);
partials_[i] = partial1;
i++;
}
if (!stan::is_constant<T2>::value) {
operands_[i] = *(vari**)(&operand2);
partials_[i] = partial2;
i++;
}
if (!stan::is_constant<T3>::value) {
operands_[i] = *(vari**)(&operand3);
partials_[i] = partial3;
}
}

void chain() {
for (size_t i = 0; i < nvars_; i++)
operands_[i]->adj_ += adj_ * partials_[i];
}
};

This changes the basic idea of the class—instead of being a class
definition with exactly 3 var operands, it's a class definition with a
maximum of 3 operands. Which means you don't have to be so careful
when defining the corresponding simple_var() function:

double extract_vari(double v) { return v; }
agrad::vari* extract_vari(const var v) { return v.vi_; }

template <typename T>
struct var_to_vi {
typedef T type;
};
template <>
struct var_to_vi<stan::agrad::var> {
typedef stan::agrad::vari* type;
};

template <typename T1, typename T2, typename T3>
inline agrad::var simple_var(double v,
const T1& y1, double dy1,
const T2& y2, double dy2,
const T3& y3, double dy3) {
return agrad::var(new agrad::partials3_vari<typename
stan::var_to_vi<T1>::type,
typename stan::var_to_vi<T2>::type,
typename stan::var_to_vi<T3>::type>(v,
extract_vari(y1), dy1,
extract_vari(y2), dy2,
extract_vari(y3), dy3));
}

Admittedly, the var_to_vi and extract_vari business isn't that pretty,
but you only have to do it once. Extending this construction to
partials4_vari would only involve a small amount of copying and
pasting, rather than implementing 16 simple_var classes.

As for the second part, I'm playing with a metaprogramming view-based
approach that I think may give most of the best of both worlds. The
idea is that you wrap scalars in a class for which operator[] just
gives you the scalar back. Then you proceed as though everything were
a vector. Assuming the compiler optimizes away the [] calls, shouldn't
cause a performance hit, I think.

Matt

parts:
Nice! We'll have this down to one big ugly
function in no time! (One big ugly function
is better than 2**N ugly functions any time.)

I added a bunch of comments inline below.

(Oh, and while we're on the topic, I realized we
only needed one set of PropTo and Policy inference
top-level template functions in normal.hpp; I
keep forgetting you can just template out whole
vectors and still use them -- you just couldn't do
that with Java generics.)

On 6/22/12 5:52 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> It's true that you can't template out variable declarations, so
> instead I used arrays whose lengths are known at compile time. The
> partials3_vari class illustrates the basic idea:
>
> template<typename T1, typename T2, typename T3>
> class partials3_vari : public vari {
> private:
> const static size_t nvars_ = !stan::is_constant<T1>::value +
> !stan::is_constant<T2>::value +
> !stan::is_constant<T3>::value;
> vari* operands_[nvars_];
> double partials_[nvars_];

I hadn't thought of using arrays of arrays
for values in the partials classes. I think it
will be transparent at compile time assuming
static member variables behave the same way as
program-level globals. But the pointer addition
will remain compared to fixed member variables.

I have toyed with just using a single partials_vari
class -- you could then push the templates down
to the constructors. But I don't see how to do it
AND keep the static compilation of nvars_.

The metaprogram calcluating nvars_ could be coded
recursively with typelists, so assignment would look like.

nvars_ = size_of<tlist<T1,tlist<T2,T3> >::value;

> public:
> partials3_vari(double value,
> T1 operand1, double partial1,
> T2 operand2, double partial2,
> T3 operand3, double partial3)
> : vari(value) {
> size_t i = 0;
> if (!stan::is_constant<T1>::value) {
> operands_[i] = *(vari**)(&operand1);
> partials_[i] = partial1;
> i++;
> }

The increment of i++ is the key to working with a single
array. Also, it's agnostic about the number of loops
it sees.

This is where you'd do the expression template trick of
wrapping a single agrad::var in a template expression
class to return itself (what in Eigen is the Matrix::Constant
method, which returns such an expression template).

struct constant_vec {
const agrad::var var_;
constant_vec(const agrad::var& var) : var_(var) { }
var operator[](size_t n) {
return var_;
}
size_t size() const { return 1; } // ?? may call operator[] with any n
};

I wrote this out because I'm not sure what the best way
to do this is. If we stay in scope, the var_ could be
a reference as could the return of operator[].

This is definitely the simplest thing to do, but there's
the overhead of constructing the constant_vec and the
function call to operator[] (which at least is not virtual).

And then the assignment is going to be in a loop, which also
won't be free (well, who knows -- the upper size bound of 1
should be known at compile time because it's a constant_vec

The other way to do this I've been toying with would be
to do static ifs with dummy wrappers.
For vectors of agrad::var, we could add an else condition:

size_t i = 0;
if (stan::is_var<T1>::value) {
operands_[i] = *(vari**)(&to_var(operand1));
partials_[i] = to_val(partial1);
i++;
} else if (stan::is_var_vec<T1>::value) {
for (size_t n = 0; n < to_vec_var(operand1).size(); ++n)
operands_[i] = *(vari**)(&to_vec_var(operand1)[n]);
partials_[i] = to_vec_val(partial1)[n];
++i;
}
}

I think this is incredibly ugly, but it might be more efficient.
The wrappers are all overloaded simple inlines, like

inline const var& to_var(const var& x) { return x; }

inline const var& to_var(const vector<var>& x) { throw ...; }

The first should be called, but compiled away.
The second will never actually be called. It's just there
to make sure &to_var(operand1) is of the right type.

The other wrappers to_val, and to_vec_var and to_vec_val
are all similar.

> if (!stan::is_constant<T2>::value) {
> operands_[i] = *(vari**)(&operand2);
> partials_[i] = partial2;
> i++;
> }
> if (!stan::is_constant<T3>::value) {
> operands_[i] = *(vari**)(&operand3);
> partials_[i] = partial3;
> }
> }
>
> void chain() {
> for (size_t i = 0; i< nvars_; i++)
> operands_[i]->adj_ += adj_ * partials_[i];
> }
> };
>
> This changes the basic idea of the classï¿½instead of being a class

> definition with exactly 3 var operands, it's a class definition with a
> maximum of 3 operands.

Right. I had coded that choice in the simple_vars call
and then in variants on partials for 1, 2, or 3 vars.
This blows out combinatorially.

If we had the C++11 template defaults for functions,
I'm thinking we could reduce this to a single class.

Another way to reduce it to a single class is to have
static dummy parameters that are ignored (or less efficiently,
ones that are zero-size expression templates for vectors).

> Which means you don't have to be so careful
> when defining the corresponding simple_var() function:

> double extract_vari(double v) { return v; }
> agrad::vari* extract_vari(const var v) { return v.vi_; }
>
> template<typename T>

> return agrad::var(new agrad::partials3_vari<typename
> stan::var_to_vi<T1>::type,
> typename stan::var_to_vi<T2>::type,
> typename stan::var_to_vi<T3>::type>(v,
> extract_vari(y1), dy1,

> extract_vari(y3), dy3));
> }
>
> Admittedly, the var_to_vi and extract_vari business isn't that pretty,

You could put the var_to_vi stuff on the partials class side,
but I don't see how to make it go away.

Also, I think we may pick up a bit of overhead in
passing variables we don't need. I'm not sure how good
the compiler is at this.

I used a similar trick in reverse to pull out the values
to compute the log prob and derivatives.

> but you only have to do it once. Extending this construction to
> partials4_vari would only involve a small amount of copying and
> pasting, rather than implementing 16 simple_var classes.

Right -- this is the big payoff.

It's like a game of whack a mole where
you managed to whack two moles down simultaneously.

> As for the second part, I'm playing with a metaprogramming view-based
> approach that I think may give most of the best of both worlds. The
> idea is that you wrap scalars in a class for which operator[] just
> gives you the scalar back. Then you proceed as though everything were
> a vector. Assuming the compiler optimizes away the [] calls, shouldn't

parts:
Hi all,

I've pushed a new branch called "vectorized" to github that implements
full vectorization/specialization for the normal in a way that should
hopefully be reasonably easy to port to other distributions (or other
functions). It includes a version of rats called rats_vec.stan that
demonstrates one way to take advantage of the vectorization. This new
version takes about 3.2 seconds to generate 10000 samples (plus 1000
warmup samples), compared to the previous (partially vectorized)
version's 4.4 seconds. By contrast, my handwritten autodiff-free
implementation of rats takes about 1.65 seconds. And JAGS takes about
1.3 seconds (although a lot of that's inefficient I/O). In summary:
JAGS 1.3
handwritten 1.7
fully vectorized 3.2
partially vec'ed 4.4
unspecialized 19.1
We've come a long way towards eliminating our autodiff overhead in the
past few weeks!

Bob, we can talk about merging this into the main branch tomorrow, perhaps?

Matt

parts:
Quick update: turns out that a minor change to rats_vec.stan actually
makes it significantly faster. The new version only takes 2.6s on
rats.

Also, if I comment out the body of check_range() and the calls to
check_finite() etc. then that goes down to 2.1s. So we're currently
paying something like a 25% overhead for that safety. It'd be nice to
have a way to disable at least the bound checking as a command line
feature, but it's surprisingly tricky to implement; the issue is that
you basically need two compiled versions of the model, one doing bound
checking and the other not. Which probably means significantly longer
compile times, which might not even be worth it.

Anyway, the main point is that we're capable of getting within about a
factor of 2 of JAGS's efficiency on its home turf (very low
correlation between parameters and full conditional conjugacy).

Matt

>> On Sunday, June 24, 2012 6:56:53 PM UTC-4, Matt Hoffman wrote:
>>>
>>> Also, if I comment out the body of check_range() and the calls to
>>> check_finite() etc. then that goes down to 2.1s. So we're currently
>>> paying something like a 25% overhead for that safety.

You can save a bit of time by moving the checks out
of the loop so that the scale parameter is only checked once.
There are already vectorized versions that
should work on either values or vectors of values.

>>> It'd be nice to
>>> have a way to disable at least the bound checking as a command line
>>> feature, but it's surprisingly tricky to implement;
>>> the issue is that
>>> you basically need two compiled versions of the model, one doing bound
>>> checking and the other not. Which probably means significantly longer
>>> compile times, which might not even be worth it.
>>
Right -- the disable-checks flag will have to be available at compile time.

>> I suspect the overhead is much worse for multivariate models. I think it is
>> easy to fold these checks into the same mechanism that Eigen uses to
>> {dis,en}able range checking, depending on whether -DNDEBUG is passed.
>>

NDEBUG is a built-in C++ macro for turning off asserts. It's apparently
handled differently than other macros by the compiler in that it
can be redefined in a single translation unit.

The bounds checking in the distributions now is based on Boost's
math error handling pattern, which is not based on assert. It's designed
to allow the behavior of compound functions to do the right thing (e.g.,
return NaN vs. throw an exception vs. write to an error log and return NaN, etc.)
So they're not set up with a way to be turned off.

If we turn these errors off, user code may segfault or just return NaN
depending on how the other functions behave in the face of illegal
inputs (e.g., sqrt of a negative number).

To turn off our checks if NDEBUG is defined, use

if (!NDEBUG) {
… error checks ...
}

The main downside is that we can't now turn off Eigen checks
and leave our own in place.

Another alternative would be to add another template param
such as:

template <… ,bool DISABLED = stan::error_checks_disabled>
check_finite(…) {
if (DISABLED) return;
}

Then we just need to make sure stan::error_checks_disabled is
a static constant defined before the probability functions.

Of course, the template default for a function is a purely C++11 thing.

One option would be to move them all to be static class methods:

template <bool DISABLED = false>
class tests {
static S check_finite(…) {
if (DISABLED) return;
….
}
};

Then the usage is, e.g., tests<DISABLED>::check_finite(….).
This is assuming we make all the tests just cover doubles
and not agrad::var.

In retrospect, it might've been better to do the probability functions
this way, too. It would've saved us some redundancy. It's not too late
to change, of course. I think it might even make the usage neater,
as in:

template <bool PropTo = false, typename Policy = default_policy>
class normal {
template <typename T_y, typename T_loc, typename T_scale>
log_prob(const T_y& y, const T_loc& mu, const T_scale& sigma) { … }
cumulative_distribution(…) { … }
}


- Bob
